title: What if…
lede: Three decisions where the story could have gone differently. The “What if” panels are speculation, labeled as such.

forks.actual: The new formula took the old one’s name and place, and production of the original stopped.[^3][^7] Only after 79 days did the company offer both.[^1][^6] A later account says it had feared that two sugar colas would split its share and let Pepsi claim first place.[^16]
forks.whatif: Launched as a second cola beside the original, the new formula would have been one more line extension in a year that also had Cherry Coke.[^22] There would have been no loss to protest and far less attention. On the evidence of what happened after July, it would probably have settled at a few share points, which is where it ended up anyway.

forks.actual: In June the company was still citing 110 million triers, 80% willing to buy again and an 18-month plan that would show the degree of acceptance “by the end of 1986.”[^5] A month later it reversed.[^6] Warren Buffett later recalled that Goizueta “just didn’t want to admit that they were wrong.”[^28]
forks.whatif: The complaints might have faded as the old stock ran out and the hoarders gave up. Or bottlers and retailers, who heard from customers every day, might have forced the issue anyway. An outside survey already had 59% of tasters preferring the original.[^6] Waiting would have risked a slower and less forgivable version of the same retreat.

forks.actual: Coca-Cola kept the new formula on sale as “Coke,” gave it its own campaign, renamed it Coke II in a 1990 test and let it shrink for years.[^1][^13][^16]
forks.whatif: Pulling it in July 1985 would have ended the story cleanly and made the reversal look total. It would also have conceded that the research was worthless. Keeping it let the company say that it had added a choice, at the price of a slow, quiet failure nobody had to announce.
